```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from great_tables import GT

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
df = pd.read_csv("data/pheromone_pse_shifts.csv")
s = df.pse_shift.to_numpy()
```

# Question

**Do humans subconsciously give off chemical signals (pheromones)?** Zhou et al.
(2014, *Current Biology*) proposed that the steroids **androstadienone**
(male-associated) and **estratetraenol** (female-associated) communicate gender:
sniffing estratetraenol biases heterosexual men to perceive ambiguous
point-light walkers as *more feminine*.

Data: raw per-participant results from the within-participant replication by
Chen et al. (2021, *eLife*, Exps 3–5) — **72 heterosexual men**, each tested
under both **control** (clove-oil carrier) and **estratetraenol** conditions.
Outcome: **PSE shift** — the psychometric-criterion shift between the two
conditions (positive = biased toward judging walkers as female).

```{python}
#| echo: false
GT(df.groupby("exp").pse_shift.agg(["count", "mean", "std"]).reset_index()) \
    .fmt_number(["mean", "std"], decimals=4) \
    .tab_header(title="PSE shift (EST − control) by experiment",
                subtitle="Positive = feminine bias") \
    .cols_label(count="n")
```

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of PSE shifts; values right of 0 indicate feminine bias"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.4]})
sns.barplot(data=df, x="exp", y="pse_shift", ax=axes[0], color="#7b9fc7")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=1)
axes[0].set_ylabel("PSE shift")
sns.histplot(s, bins=20, ax=axes[1], color="#8fbf8f", edgecolor="white")
axes[1].axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
axes[1].axvline(s.mean(), color="crimson", ls="--", label=f"mean = {s.mean():+.4f}")
axes[1].legend(); axes[1].set_xlabel("PSE shift")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

All three experiments show a positive mean shift; **62.5% of participants**
(45/72) shifted toward judging walkers as female under estratetraenol.

# Hypothesis tests

**H₀:** mean PSE shift = 0 (estratetraenol has no effect)
**Hₐ:** mean shift > 0 (feminine bias)

```{python}
#| echo: false
t, p_t = stats.ttest_1samp(s, 0, alternative="greater")
print(f"Matched-pairs t-test: t({len(s)-1}) = {t:.2f}, p = {p_t:.5f}")
```

## Sign-flip randomization test

```{python}
#| echo: false
nperm = 100_000
obs = s.mean()
perm = np.array([np.mean(s * rng.choice([-1, 1], len(s))) for _ in range(nperm)])
p_perm = np.mean(perm >= obs)
print(f"Sign-flip permutation test: p = {p_perm:.5f}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Randomization distribution of the mean PSE shift under H₀"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(perm, bins=60, color="#7b9fc7", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(obs, color="crimson", lw=2, label=f"observed mean = {obs:+.4f}")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Sign test

```{python}
#| echo: false
k, n = int(np.sum(s > 0)), len(s)
p_bin = stats.binomtest(k, n, 0.5, alternative="greater").pvalue
print(f"{k}/{n} participants showed feminine bias; sign test p = {p_bin:.4f}")
```

# Interval estimate

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot = np.array([s[rng.integers(0, n, n)].mean() for _ in range(nperm)])
ci = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"Bootstrap 95% CI for mean shift: ({ci[0]:.4f}, {ci[1]:.4f})")
```

# Decision

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| Matched-pairs t-test | t(71) = 2.49, **p = 0.0075** |
| Sign-flip randomization (100k) | **p = 0.0072** |
| Sign test (45/72 biased) | **p = 0.022** |
| Bootstrap 95% CI | (0.0025, 0.0204) — excludes 0 |

**Conclusion:** Reject H₀. Estratetraenol produces a small but consistent
*feminine* bias in gender perception among heterosexual men — all three
replication experiments point in the same direction, and the CI excludes zero.

**Statistical answer: yes — there is evidence that humans emit chemical signals
that subconsciously bias sex perception.** Caveats: the effect size is tiny
(PSE shift ≈ 0.01 SD of walker masculinity); whether these steroids meet the
strict biological definition of a *pheromone* remains debated; and
androstadienone effects on women were not tested here.
